#4732. Sykeruns X7 electric dirt bike review: A lot of power for surprisingly little money

The mini electric dirt bike market has exploded over the last few years, with seemingly countless new brands offering everything from pint-sized electric pit bikes to surprisingly powerful off-road machines. The Sykeruns X7 falls somewhere in the middle, offering enough power to get into some serious trouble while keeping the price relatively approachable.

I’ve spent some time now riding the X7, and while it certainly isn’t the most refined electric dirt bike I’ve tested, there’s enough to like about what you’re getting for the money.

In fact, if you’re looking for a reasonably powerful electric dirt bike for recreational trail riding without spending several thousand dollars, this might be worth a closer look.

The Sykeruns X7 is a compact electric dirt bike featuring a 5,500W peak-rated motor, which translates to around 7.4 horsepower. That’s quite a bit of power for a bike at this price point of $1,699, especially considering that many similarly priced electric two-wheelers are significantly less powerful. Oh, and for our readers, we’ve gotten you set up with a 20% discount. Just use code ELECTREK20 to drop the price down to an impressive $1,359!

Sykeruns claims a top speed of 57 mph (92 km/h), though since this is an off-road only bike, you’ll rarely get the chance to put that claim to the test. I certainly didn’t, as I didn’t have a long enough and flat enough stretch of trail where I felt comfortable hitting nearly highway speeds on a low-cost e-moto.

The battery is a 60V 27Ah pack, providing 1,620 Wh of capacity. Sykeruns claims up to 60 miles (96 km) of range, though as with virtually every electric dirt bike, your actual range will depend heavily on how aggressively you’re riding. Fast trail riding, steep climbs, and repeated hard acceleration can eat through battery capacity much more quickly than leisurely cruising. Suffice it to say that you’ll likely not see the 60 mile figure in real world scenarios, but that’s still a fairly large battery.

The bike rolls on a 17-inch front wheel and 14-inch rear wheel, both wrapped in knobby off-road tires. Hydraulic disc brakes handle stopping duties, while an inverted suspension fork and rear monoshock help smooth out the bumps.

At 143 lb (65 kg), the X7 isn’t exactly featherweight, but it’s also far from being a full-size electric motorcycle.

The first thing I was surprised about with the X7 is that it offers a pretty decent amount of performance for the money. There’s enough power here to have some real fun, and the bike doesn’t feel like one of those underpowered mini electric motorcycles that struggles once you get beyond casual neighborhood speeds.

That said, I wouldn’t describe the acceleration as mind-blowing, either. We’re not talking about the kind of explosive power delivery you’d get from a high-end electric dirt bike costing several times as much. Instead, the X7 delivers a healthy amount of acceleration that feels appropriate for a recreational off-road machine.

And let’s be real here, that’s probably what most people shopping in this budget category are looking for.

The suspension is another area where the X7 earns a passing grade without necessarily winning any awards. The front fork and rear shock do their jobs, absorbing the bumps and ruts you’d expect to encounter on typical trails. It’s nothing I’d call plush, but I could see it doing light jumps with minimal air time.

Would I want to take this thing to a motocross track and start launching it off massive jumps? Not particularly. The suspension doesn’t have the premium feel or sophisticated damping of more expensive machines.

But for general trail riding, exploring dirt roads, and the occasional overlanding shenanigans, it’s perfectly serviceable. Not every electric dirt bike needs to be a competition-ready machine, and the X7 seems comfortable occupying that more recreational category.

I was also pleasantly surprised by the tires, which seem well suited to the bike’s intended purpose. The knobby tread offers a reasonable amount of grip for off-road riding, and I didn’t find myself immediately wishing for a tire upgrade.

The overall size is worth mentioning, too. This isn’t a particularly large electric dirt bike, but at my modest 5’7” (170 cm) height, I felt comfortable on it. The riding position didn’t feel overly cramped, and the bike was manageable enough that I didn’t feel like I was wrestling with an oversized machine.

Taller riders might find it a bit more compact than they’d prefer, but for average-height riders, the proportions seem reasonable.

If there’s one area where the X7 reminds you of its budget-friendly $1,699 price tag, it’s the overall level of refinement.

Nothing about the bike struck me as particularly premium. The components, finishes, and general construction are more in line with what I’d expect from a relatively inexpensive electric dirt bike.

But that’s not necessarily a criticism. There’s a difference between something feeling inexpensive and something feeling inadequate, and the X7 generally stays on the acceptable side of that line.

The controls are straightforward, the digital display provides the basic information you need, and the overall package feels focused on delivering usable performance rather than impressing riders with fancy features.

The grippy hydraulic brakes are also a welcome inclusion, especially considering the speeds this bike is capable of reaching. With a machine that can approach highway speeds, having proper motorcycle-style braking hardware is important.

Of course, long-term durability is a separate question. Budget electric dirt bikes don’t always have the same track record, parts availability, or established dealer networks as the more recognizable motorcycle brands. That’s something worth considering before purchasing, particularly if you plan to ride hard or frequently.

One thing I appreciate about the Sykeruns X7 is that the company makes its intended use fairly clear.

There’s a large red warning sticker on the bike explaining that it’s intended for off-road use only. That’s a good thing, especially in today’s market, where the lines between electric bicycles, electric dirt bikes, and electric motorcycles are becoming increasingly blurred, despite laws existing to keep these types of bikes out of the bike lane and off of public roads.

The X7 is absolutely not an electric bicycle. It doesn’t have pedals, it produces several thousand watts of power, and it’s capable of speeds far beyond anything permitted under electric bicycle regulations.

It’s an off-road electric motorcycle, plain and simple.

Interestingly, though, Sykeruns has equipped the bike with features like a tail light and turn signals, which could potentially give some riders the wrong impression.

Those are certainly useful features on a motorcycle, but they don’t magically make a vehicle street legal. Without the necessary certification, registration, and other road-use requirements, the X7 remains an off-road-only machine.

I worry that some buyers might see those lights and assume they can ride the bike around town like a small electric motorcycle. That’s not the case, and it’s important to understand that distinction before buying one.

After spending time with the Sykeruns X7, my biggest takeaway is that this is a reasonably capable electric dirt bike at a pretty compelling price.

It’s not the best electric dirt bike I’ve ever ridden. The suspension is fairly basic, the build quality is unremarkable, and there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about the design.

But for $1,699 (or $1,359 if you use the code ELECTREK20 to take 20% off!), you’re getting a 5.5 kW peak-rated electric motorcycle with a sizable battery, proper off-road tires, hydraulic brakes, and enough performance to have some genuine fun on the trails.

I wouldn’t say that the X7 here is trying to compete with more up-market electric dirt bikes from the likes of Juiced, Sur-Ron or Talaria on overall refinement, but they make this type of riding much more accessible.

And that’s really where I think the X7 makes the most sense.

If you’re an experienced dirt bike rider looking for a highly refined machine with excellent suspension and premium components, you’ll probably want to keep shopping.

But if you’re someone who wants a fun electric dirt bike for exploring private property, cruising around trails where motorized riding is permitted, or just enjoying some recreational off-road riding without spending a fortune, the Sykeruns X7 offers a pretty reasonable package.

It doesn’t need to be amazing at everything. At this price, being pretty good at most things is already an accomplishment.

#4730. The best pizza ovens

Updated Oct 26, 2026 10:20 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

The best pizza oven for most people is the Gozney Arc ($799.99 at Gozney as of October 2026), a 14-inch propane oven with a thermometer in the box that I’ve cooked on myself. If space or budget is tight, its smaller sibling, the Gozney Arc Lite ($399.99), heats quickly, holds its heat, and packs away easily. If you’d rather cook over live fire, the Ooni Karu 2 ($449) burns wood or charcoal out of the box. Plenty has changed since our last update: Gozney replaced the Dome we tested with the Dome Gen 2, Ooni renamed the Karu 12G to Karu 2 and put our old favorite, the first-generation Karu 12, on clearance, Ooni now sells a stone that rotates your pizza for you, and the ALFA oven we recommended for big pies is discontinued. This guide covers outdoor ovens plus one indoor pick; if you only cook inside, our guide to the best indoor pizza ovens goes deeper.

I’ve cooked on the Gozney Arc and Arc Lite myself, and PopSci tested the Ninja Woodfire, the Nexgrill Ora, and the original Gozney Dome for earlier versions of this guide. The rest of the picks are research-based. We didn’t run a new comparative test round for this update. Instead, we combined our earlier hands-on testing with current manufacturer specs and measurements from named independent reviewers, and we focused on heat-up time, cooking consistency, ease of use, capacity, and fire management.

For the researched picks, we read the manufacturers’ spec pages and help centers, checked every price at a named retailer on October 21, 2026, and read reviews from TechRadar, T3, Livingetc, and Bob Vila, crediting their measurements by name. Maximum temperatures are labeled as manufacturer ratings because a stone rarely reaches them in use. We also checked each brand’s lineup for successors and discontinued models, which is how the old Dome, the first-generation Karu 12, and the ALFA 4 Pizze ended up reworked or cut.

We favored ovens you can buy new from the manufacturer or a major retailer today, and we cut picks that only turned up through third-party sellers, which is what happened to our old countertop pick.

Pizza ovens split along fuel lines. Propane is the easiest to live with, wood and charcoal require more attention but give you a live-fire cooking experience, and electric models trade top-end heat for convenience. Our picks range from $149 to $2,299.99 and cover all three, plus an indoor oven. Maximum temperatures are manufacturer ratings, and each card’s specs list how we evaluated it: tested, researched, or predecessor tested (we tested the previous version and researched the current one).

Prices and availability were checked from October 21 to October 26, 2026, at the retailers named and may change.

Why it won: The Gozney Arc keeps the rolling side flame of the Arc Lite but adds room for 14-inch pies, a thicker stone, and a thermometer in the box.

I’ve cooked on both of Gozney’s compact Arc ovens, and the regular Gozney Arc is the one I’d recommend first. It costs $799.99 at Gozney, twice the price of the Arc Lite below, and the extra money addresses the Lite’s two biggest limits: the Arc takes a 14-inch pizza instead of a 12-inch one, and it comes with a thermometer, so you’re not guessing at the oven’s temperature.

On paper, the rest of the upgrade is about holding heat. Gozney lists a 20mm cordierite stone, thicker than the Arc Lite’s 12mm, inside a two-layer insulated body, and that extra stone mass is what you want when you’re launching pizzas back to back. The heat comes from a lateral gas burner on one side that Gozney says recreates a wood-fired rolling flame, the same layout as the Lite, with an adjustable flame control. The box also includes a hose and regulator for a standard propane tank, a burner guard, and a stone adjustment tool.

The tradeoff is bulk. Gozney lists the Arc at 47.5 pounds and about 19 by 22 inches, nearly twice the Arc Lite’s weight, so it’s still a tabletop oven but less of a grab-it-and-go one. It runs on propane only, and Gozney extends the warranty from one year to five if you register within 60 days. The built-in thermometer reads the oven, not the stone, so an infrared thermometer is still useful. If you want 16-inch pies, the Arc XL costs $999.99.

Why it won: The Arc Lite heats fast and holds its heat in a 26.4-pound body that costs half as much as the Arc.

I’ve been cooking on the Gozney Arc Lite too, and it’s the one I’d pick if storage space or budget matters more than pie size. It heats up quickly, it holds that heat well from one pizza to the next, and it cools down relatively quickly once you turn off the gas, which matters when you’re the one waiting to put it away. It also feels like a much more expensive oven than it is. Gozney launched the Arc Lite in March 2026 at $399.99, which is still its price (it dropped to $349.99 during Gozney’s Labor Day sale).

Size is the reason it gets its own slot. Gozney lists it at 26.4 pounds and about 17 by 19 inches, with a half-inch cordierite stone sized for 12-inch pies and a rolling flame along one side of the chamber, controlled by a dial on the front. It fits on a small patio table or a shelf in the garage between cooks. That footprint may also suit some balconies, provided your building rules, local restrictions, and Gozney’s clearance requirements permit a propane oven. Bob Vila’s reviewer, writing in May 2026, needed 20 to 30 minutes of preheat and finished most pizzas in 2 to 3 minutes.

My one real gripe is the missing thermometer. The Arc Lite has no built-in temperature readout, so you can’t see when the stone is ready, and an infrared thermometer is strongly recommended if you want repeatable results. Gozney sells its own infrared thermometer for $49.99, and our guide to the best infrared thermometers has other options. Gozney offers an extensive accessory lineup (covers, a stand shared with the bigger Arc models, peels), although the extras add up quickly. If you want 14-inch pies and a thermometer in the box, step up to the Arc above; the Arc XL goes to 16 inches for $999.99.

Why it won: The Karu 2 burns wood or charcoal out of the box and takes a $120 gas burner later, so you don’t have to pick a fuel up front.

Propane is the easy way to make pizza. Wood is the more involved way, and the Ooni Karu 2 is the oven we’d buy for it. It burns hardwood or charcoal right out of the box, and the optional gas burner (a $120 add-on) gives you propane for weeknights when you don’t feel like tending a fire. Ooni lists it at $449. If the name is new to you, it shouldn’t be: Ooni’s own FAQ says the Karu 12G and the Karu 2 are the exact same oven, so the Karu 2 is a rename, not a redesign.

Wood takes more attention than gas. You’re feeding small splits into the rear tray, watching the flame, and adjusting airflow to keep the stone hot, and how close you get to Ooni’s 950°F rating depends on dry fuel and a well-fed fire. The Karu 2’s built-in thermometer tracks the oven temperature, but an infrared thermometer is still useful because it tells you when the stone itself is ready for a pizza. Live fire can add some smoke character, especially on longer cooks, though for a pizza that bakes in about a minute or two the difference versus gas may be subtle. Most of the appeal is the fire itself.

Our previous best overall, the first-generation Ooni Karu 12, is still on sale at Ooni for $249 (down from $349). At 26.5 pounds, it’s lighter and $200 cheaper than the Karu 2, and it’s a good buy while the clearance stock lasts.

Why it won: The Dome Gen 2 adds a built-in air-and-floor temperature console and room for a 16-inch pie to the design we tested.

We tested the original Gozney Dome for an earlier version of this guide, and it impressed us. In gas mode it passed 930°F in under 20 minutes without any tending, and it took us three or four pies to dial in a classic Neapolitan, after which it was easy to repeat. That Dome is gone now. Gozney replaced it with the Dome Gen 2 in fall 2025, its old product link now forwards to the Gen 2 lineup, and Gozney’s help center says the cheaper Dome S1 is no longer made. What follows about the Gen 2 comes from Gozney’s specs and other outlets’ reviews, not our own testing.

The Gen 2 is a bigger, smarter oven. Gozney’s specs call for one 16-inch pizza or two 10-inch pies on a 30mm cordierite stone, 136.7 pounds for the oven alone, and a built-in digital console that shows air and floor temperature, runs a cook timer, and takes two meat probes. It comes in separate propane and natural-gas versions and can also burn wood or charcoal. Gozney’s optional Wood-Fire Control Kit ($199.99, sold out when we checked) adds powered airflow and finer control over a live fire. Gas mode works a lot like a propane grill: light it, then manage the pizza’s distance from the flame.

It’s a project, though, and the stand is extra. TechRadar’s December 2025 review lists a 40- to 45-minute heat time, says the oven does best with little or no wind blowing into the mouth, and notes that the Gen 2 drops the original’s steam injector attachment for bread. T3’s reviewer couldn’t get the igniter to spark even after two battery changes and lit it with a match instead. It was $1,999.99 during Gozney’s Labor Day sale, and the Dome XL Gen 2 fits an 18-inch pie for $2,799.99.

Why it won: We tested the Ninja Woodfire, and it’s the only pick here with a built-in pellet smoker and a dehydrate mode.

We love pizza as much as the next person, but you have to eat something else occasionally, and the Ninja Woodfire 8-in-1 Outdoor Oven handles most of it. It’s about the size of a microwave and runs on electricity. You plug it in, add the right rack or the pizza stone, set the temperature, and let it preheat. Next to the gas and wood ovens on this list, it’s close to hands-off.

It has five pizza settings: thin crust, pan, New York, Neapolitan, and frozen. In our testing, the Neapolitan and New York modes took about 15 minutes to hit max temperature, then we slid in the pizza and closed the door. There’s almost no learning curve and no turning or babysitting, and when we opened the door we had a well-cooked pie. The chamber is snug, though. Our roughly 12-inch pizza just barely fit and took some nudging to keep it from oozing over the sides. The stone lifts out, but Ninja says not to get it wet: let it cool completely, scrape it gently with a nonmetal tool, and wipe away debris with a soft cloth.

Once you’re done with pizza, it roasts, broils, bakes, dehydrates, and smokes. It held a steady 225°F to 250°F in our testing, and the pellet box on the side adds smoke flavor the way a pellet grill does. SharkNinja’s own store showed the Woodfire out of stock at its $399.99 list price, while Best Buy had it for $329.99 with a 4.1-star average across 864 ratings. SharkNinja’s newer Ninja Artisan MO201 ($249.99 on sale, down from $299.99) keeps the 12-inch capacity and 700°F ceiling but drops the pellet smoker.

Why it won: For $149, the Nexgrill Ora’s rotating-stone knob gave us a more even bake than turning pies by hand.

Cooking homemade pizza in a 900°F oven can be intimidating, and the Nexgrill Ora 12 makes it easier to get good results on your first try. A knob on the right side rotates the central pizza stone, turning your pie for an even cook. With most ovens, you turn the pizza yourself with a peel, and at these temperatures 10 seconds can be the difference between a well-cooked pizza and a charred one.

Setup was easy. The oven comes fully assembled; all we had to do was drop in the five pieces of its stone, which felt like a big, easy puzzle, then connect a propane tank. Gas is beginner-friendly because the heat is steady without feeding wood. A chamber on top can hold wood if you want a little smoke. Turning it on was as simple as twisting the power knob to the flame icon. The flame sits toward the back, so rotating matters, and the oven was ready in about 10 minutes in our testing (Nexgrill rates it to reach 900°F in about 20). Our one complaint is the lack of a built-in thermometer.

Pizzas went in and out the same way as in other ovens: flour the dough on a peel, top it lightly, launch it, and pull it after about 90 to 120 seconds. The difference was a more even cook every time, thanks to the knob, which has enough resistance that you won’t send the pie spinning. Nexgrill sells it for $149, though The Home Depot listed it at $206.12 the same day, where it averages 3.9 stars across 116 reviews and a couple of owners mention the knob occasionally sticking.

Why it won: The Koda 2 Max is rated for a 20-inch pie or three 10-inch pizzas at once for about $1,000 less than the Dome Gen 2.

Feeding a backyard full of people one 12-inch pie at a time gets old fast. The Ooni Koda 2 Max is our pick for that party. Ooni rates its 24-by-21-inch cordierite stone for one 20-inch New York-style pie, two 12-inch pizzas, or three 10-inch pizzas at once, and two independently controlled burners let you run the two sides at different heat.

It’s gas only, in separate propane and natural-gas versions, and Ooni includes its Connect digital temperature hub and a food probe, so you’re not guessing at stone temperature the way you are with the Arc Lite. We replaced the ALFA 4 Pizze with it in this slot. The ALFA we used to link is discontinued, and the current wood-fired top ran about $2,800 to $3,000 at BBQGuys and Embers Living, before you build a base for it.

At 95 pounds, it needs a permanent spot on a stout table. Ooni lists it at $1,299, though the page showed it out of stock with preorders open, so check the delivery estimate before you plan a party around it. It also works with Ooni’s rotating stone, sold separately or in a $1,649 bundle.

Why it won: This is the least expensive way to get Ooni’s motorized stone, which turns the pizza so you don’t have to.

Turning the pizza is the skill that separates a leopard-spotted crust from a scorched one, and Ooni’s rotating stone takes it off your plate. Launched in March 2026, it replaces the standard stone in Ooni’s Koda 2 ovens with a motor-driven one powered by a battery pack under the oven floor. Wave your hand or a peel in front of its sensor and it starts or stops. Ooni says it can spin continuously or turn 90 degrees at timed intervals, and that four AA batteries last about seven hours of rotation.

We picked the bundle with the standard 14-inch Koda 2 because it’s the least expensive of Ooni’s three rotating-stone bundles: $799 (regular $828), versus $499 for the oven alone and $329 for the 12-inch stone on its own. You still launch the pizza yourself. Livingetc’s reviewer, writing in May 2026, got an uneven first pie because she moved it too soon, then got even results by turning the flame down to about half; each pizza took 90 seconds to two minutes.

The rotating stone caps the base Koda 2 at 12-inch pies (the standard stone that’s also in the box handles 14), and the base Koda 2 has no thermometer. The cheaper way to rotate is the Nexgrill Ora’s manual knob for $149. Ooni showed the bundle out of stock with preorders open, so check the ship date.

Why it won: The Volt 2 is the successor to the indoor oven we tested and liked best, and Ooni rates it for 850°F from a standard outlet.

No yard, no balcony, or no interest in standing outside in February? The Ooni Volt 2 brings high-heat pizza indoors. Ooni says it’s made for indoor use only, plugs into a standard 120-volt outlet, and reaches 850°F. It replaced the original Ooni Volt, which PopSci tested and named the top pick in our guide to the best indoor pizza ovens. We haven’t tested the Volt 2 itself, so this pick is research-based.

Ooni calls the control system Pizza Intelligence. In practice, it’s presets for Neapolitan, thin-and-crispy, and pan pizzas that manage the top and bottom elements for you, plus a Boost mode that Ooni says drives the top element hard enough for a 90-second Neapolitan. A proofing mode drops as low as 70°F for dough, and the smoke and grease filter goes in the dishwasher.

It costs $699 at Ooni, and Ooni extends the warranty to three years if you register it. The Charcoal Grey version was sold out when we checked, while Polar White was listed at the same price. At 38.8 pounds, it wants a permanent spot on the counter.

Every oven on this list can make a good pizza. The differences come down to fuel, size, and how much help you want while you learn.

Propane is the default for a reason. You turn a knob, wait for the stone to heat, and the flame stays steady all night. Wood and charcoal take more attention, since you’re feeding the fire and managing airflow; some people want that ritual, and live fire can add some smoke character, though on a pizza that bakes in a minute or two it may be subtle. Electric ovens like the Ninja Woodfire and Ooni Volt 2 are the easiest of all, though Ninja rates the Woodfire to 700°F, below the 900°F to 950°F ratings on the gas ovens here. The Dome Gen 2 and Koda 2 Max are sold in separate propane and natural-gas configurations, so choose the version that matches your setup.

A 12-inch pizza capacity is enough for most households, and it’s what keeps the Arc Lite and Karu 2 portable. The 14-inch Gozney Arc is the middle ground at 47.5 pounds. Bigger stones let you cook larger pies or several at once, but the weight climbs fast: their makers list the Koda 2 Max at 95 pounds and the Dome Gen 2 at 136.7 pounds. Measure your table, and decide whether the oven lives outside full time or goes back into storage after each cook.

Stone temperature is the key measurement for deciding when to launch a pizza, and several ovens here don’t show it. The Arc Lite, the Nexgrill Ora, and the base Koda 2 have no built-in readout, so budget about $50 for an infrared thermometer. The Karu 2, Gozney Arc, and Arc XL have built-in thermometers, the Dome Gen 2 has a digital console, and the Koda 2 Max comes with Ooni’s temperature hub, but an infrared reading of the stone is still useful on all of them.

Most outdoor ovens put the flame on one side or at the back, so the side nearest the fire cooks faster and you have to turn the pie regularly with a turning peel. If that sounds stressful, the Nexgrill Ora’s manual rotation knob and Ooni’s motorized rotating stone handle it for you.

Neapolitan-style pizza needs intense heat to cook in a couple of minutes or less, which is why most gas and wood ovens here are rated to 900°F or 950°F. Those are manufacturer ratings; the stone itself usually reads lower in use, especially on wood. In our testing, pies on the Nexgrill Ora took about 90 to 120 seconds. New York-style and pan pizzas do better a bit cooler and a bit longer.

Gas is better for most people because the heat is steady and it takes almost no fire management. Wood and charcoal are more hands-on and can add some smoke character, though on a fast-baking pizza the difference may be subtle. Multi-fuel ovens like the Ooni Karu 2 burn wood or charcoal out of the box and take an optional gas burner, so you don’t have to choose up front.

It’s strongly recommended for any oven without a built-in readout, including the Gozney Arc Lite, the Nexgrill Ora, and the base Ooni Koda 2, and it’s still useful on ovens that have one. An infrared thermometer reads the stone’s surface temperature, which is what tells you when to launch. Gozney’s costs $49.99 as of October 2026.

No. Propane, wood, and charcoal ovens burn fuel and produce carbon monoxide, so they belong outside with open air around them. Follow your oven’s manual for clearances. If you want to cook indoors, use an electric oven designed for it, like the Ooni Volt 2, which Ooni says is for indoor use only.

The Karu 12G and Karu 2 are the same oven; Ooni’s FAQ says so directly, and the Karu 2 is the current name. The Karu 12 is the first-generation model, which Ooni was selling for $249 (down from $349) as of October 2026.

The original Gozney Dome has been replaced by the Dome Gen 2, which launched in fall 2025 starting at $2,299.99, and Gozney’s old Dome product page now forwards to the Gen 2 lineup. Gozney’s help center says the Dome S1 is no longer manufactured. A larger Dome XL Gen 2 costs $2,799.99.

Yes. On July 9, 2026, the CPSC announced a recall of about 12,660 Cuisinart Propel+ Four Burner 3-in-1 Gas Grills with a pizza oven (model CGG-6331), because the oven’s tempered glass window can shatter. They were sold at Lowe’s, Walmart, and Cuisinart.com from December 2024 through May 2026. A search of the CPSC recall database on October 21, 2026, found no recalls for the specific models recommended here.

The deepest discounts we documented in 2026 came during holiday sales. During Labor Day 2026, Gozney cut the Arc Lite to $349.99 and the Dome Gen 2 to $1,999.99, and Ooni’s Memorial Day 2026 sale had the first-generation Karu 12 at $249. We’ll update this guide after Black Friday.

The Gozney Arc is the best starting point for most buyers: it takes 14-inch pies, comes with a thermometer, and costs $799.99. If space or budget is tight, the $399.99 Gozney Arc Lite heats quickly, holds its heat, and stores easily; add a $50 infrared thermometer. Choose the Ooni Karu 2 if tending a live fire is part of the appeal, the Nexgrill Ora 12 if price and easy turning matter most, or the Ooni Volt 2 if your pizza oven has to live in the kitchen. For crowds, the Ooni Koda 2 Max handles 20-inch pies, and the Gozney Dome Gen 2 is the one to build an outdoor kitchen around.

#4729. Letter From the Editor-in-Chief: What a Decade of Bedtime Stories Taught Me About Health

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

I’ve read to my children each night at bedtime for as long as I (and they) can remember. We started with the likes of “Goodnight Batcave” and the lesser-known-in-the-US but oh-so-wonderful collection of verse-driven classics from former UK Children’s Laureate Julia Donaldson.

We moved on to B.J. Novak’s anarchic love letter to the power of words (and to great typography), “The Book With No Pictures.”

We eventually worked our way up to Roald Dahl’s wickedly dark back catalog, discovering more complex characters, language and plotting as we went.

When my eldest, Amelia, hit 6, it was time to roll out the big guns.

Over the last 5 years (she’s now 11), I’ve read the seven Harry Potter books aloud twice, complete with all the voices: once to Amelia on her own, once to both her and her brother, Henry, two years her junior.

I had feared she wouldn’t be keen on another helping, but Amelia immersed herself once more in the world of Hogwarts with no hesitation and took immense joy in watching Henry discover for himself every twist and turn on Harry’s journey.

We have done the same thing with Tolkien’s “The Hobbit” and his fantasy masterpiece “The Lord of the Rings,” and are currently midway through “The Two Towers” on our second go around.

There’s a huge amount of reciprocal joy we take from this nightly ritual, beyond the practical benefits of providing a calming demarcation between the end of the day and the wind-down to sleep.

For me, it comes as either a break in my working day or a signal that it’s over, depending on how hectic things are.

For the kids, it’s an all-too-rare chance to get me all to themselves, no deadlines, screens, or other distractions to pull me away from being anything but 100% present.

For all three of us, it’s a literal (and literary!) warm blanket — a chance to escape under the covers to familiar worlds and familiar faces. It is, in short, incredibly good for our well-being.

And yet, in the world of health information — including on this site — thousands, if not millions, of reading hours are dedicated to the benefits of nutrition, sleep, and exercise as the building blocks of good health. Reading itself rarely makes that shortlist.

For me, it unequivocally deserves a place on it. Research seems to support that case. Even if we need more of it to really understand how and why.

A recent editorial in Psychological Medicine co-authored by Barbara Sahakian, Professor of Clinical Neuropsychology at Cambridge University, draws on a broad range of research linking reading for pleasure to better mental health and greater empathy.

The positive impact of reading on young people — just like Amelia and Henry — lso carries evidence.

Among more than 10,000 US adolescents, those who started reading for pleasure early had fewer mental health problems, spent less time on screens and slept more. Although, per an earlier column of mine, I can’t vouch for the sleep side of things when it comes to early bird Henry.

For many, reading can be a form of therapy that improves well-being. Bibliotherapy is a complementary therapeutic tool for emotional release and reduced stress and anxiety, with its roots traced back to ancient civilizations.

There’s even research suggesting a link between a love of reading and a lower risk of cognitive decline.

In a 2003 study of people aged 75 and over, reading was associated with a 35% lower risk of dementia over roughly five years.

A separate 14-year study from 2022 found that people who read at least weekly saw less cognitive decline, whatever their level of education.

A happy (and healthy) by-product of this love of being read to is that both my kids have now started reading to me at bedtime. Henry recently read “Jeffy the Burglar’s Cat” to us, a lesser-known but no less compelling chapter book by Ursula Moray Williams that was a staple of my own childhood. And we’ve enjoyed several books from Amelia, including the wistful tale of friendship and the circle of life, “Charlotte’s Web” by E.B. White – not a dry eye in the house for the final few chapters of that one.

They’ve also gone off and re-read the Harry Potter books and “The Hobbit” to themselves.

The research above links reading to many health benefits: better attention and memory, fewer mental health problems, more sleep, less time on screens, and greater empathy. I haven’t measured any of those impacts empirically in our house. Nor am I naive to the fact that as they get older, they’ll ultimately grow out of me reading to them, with school, extracurricular activities, their friends, and inevitably screens competing for more and more of their time.

Come what may, though, I know that a child who considers missing a reading session as the most cardinal of cardinal sins, and who scrambles for the chance to read aloud to their dad at bedtime is, at that moment, concentrating, empathizing, discovering and growing.

Researchers are clear that studies espousing the benefits of reading show association rather than proof, and it’s evident that more experimental work and deeper research are needed to ensure the complex cause and effect stands on firm scientific ground.

Regardless, it’s a healthy habit Amelia, Henry and I are very happy to keep, and with a bit of luck, I’ll get to pass it on to their kids one day.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4728. BMW is going upscale with its first 3-row EV, the iX7

BMW’s next electric SUV won’t just be bigger. The iX7 will sit at the top of the brand’s EV lineup when it debuts in 2027, bringing a more luxurious option to the mix.

After the new X5 and iX5, the X7, BMW’s biggest SUV, is due for a Neue Klasse overhaul. BMW said the second-generation X7 will arrive in 2027, including the first fully electric version, the iX7.

Ahead of its upcoming debut, camouflaged prototypes have been spotted testing, revealing a few design changes.

Although it won’t fully adopt BMW’s Neue Klasse design, like the iX3, the three-row SUV appears to feature a slimmer, more upright Kidney Grille instead of the traditional wide BMW Grille.

The iX7 also swaps conventional pull-style door handles for small handles on the vehicle’s pillar. It also retains split headlights rather than the updated Neue Klasse-style headlights on the iX3 (shown below on the right).

While BMW has yet to reveal details, a Reddit user who claims to work at BMW’s factory in South Carolina and has seen the second-generation X7 shared a few new details.

Like the X5 and iX5, the new X7 and iX7 will retain a more traditional design rather than going full-on Neue Klasse, including the Kidney Grille. The user also said BMW is dropping the split tailgate, which it did with the new X5, in favor of a standard one-piece tailgate.

Inside, the dashboard and center console are similar to the new X5, but with upgraded tech and features from the new 7 Series sedan.

BMW said the new 7 Series sedan “takes the lead when it comes to the introduction of technologies from the Neue Klasse into existing models.”

Optional features will reportedly include the upgraded 31.3″ 8K BMW Theatre Screen for rear passengers and a 14.6″ BMW Passenger Screen. It will also have optional touch screen panels on the rear doors, the user said.

While most of the claims make sense, we’ll have to wait for BMW to confirm it officially. The new X7 and iX7 are expected to debut in mid-2027.

Like the iX5 60 xDrive, the three-row iX7 is expected to use a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain. The iX5’s AWD setup delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque, enabling it to hit 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds.

The iX5 uses a massive 144 kWh battery, which BMW said offers up to 435 miles of range. It will also use an 800V electrical system for fast charging.

BMW showed just how fast it can charge during a media event in Southern California earlier this month, where the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW. With up to 460 kW peak charging, the iX5 60 xDrive can add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes, BMW says.

The new X7 and iX7 are expected to go into production at BMW’s Spartanburg plant in SC in late 2027, joining the new iX5.

#4727. The best portable chargers

Updated Oct 26, 2026 10:37 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

The best portable charger is the Anker Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W) ($229.99 at Anker as of October 2026), because it can fast-charge two laptops and a phone at once, gets back to 80 percent in 40 minutes by Anker’s rating, and stays just under the 100Wh airline limit. If you carry an iPhone, the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro ($109.99 at Anker) snaps on magnetically and charges at up to 25W with no cable, and if you want a laptop-capable bank for less, the UGREEN Nexode 20,000mAh 130W costs $59.99. Plenty has changed since our last update: our previous budget pick appears to be a model INIU recalled in December 2025, Anker recalled several of its own banks in 2025, Qi2.2 magnetic banks raised wireless charging speeds from 15W to 25W, and airlines tightened power bank rules this spring. This guide is for anyone who wants to keep a phone, tablet, or laptop running away from an outlet; if you need to power appliances or camp for a week, our guide to the best portable power stations fits better.

We’ve used power banks for years to keep phones, cameras, and laptops alive while covering events, traveling, and working away from a desk, and our own testing covered the UGREEN 145W bank here and the predecessor of our travel pick. For this update, we also read the 2026 power bank reviews and roundups from outlets including Macworld, Digital Camera World, Expert Reviews, Engadget, Tom’s Guide, and CleverHiker, logged which products independent testers kept landing on, and noted where testers disagreed with each other or with the maker’s numbers.

Then we checked every finalist against its maker’s current product page and a live retail listing on October 21, 2026. We also checked each brand’s recall history with the Consumer Product Safety Commission, which changed two of our picks. The other seven picks are researched rather than tested by us, and each section says which is which. We have a MagGo 2 Pro on the way for review and will update this guide as our own results come in.

The picks below run from a $30 pocket battery to a $250 bank with a wall outlet built in. Before you buy, know the two numbers that matter most: how much your devices draw when they charge, and whether you plan to fly with the battery. Output figures in the table are the makers’ ratings. Prices were checked on October 21, 2026 at the retailer named in each pick’s section, and power banks go on sale often, so check before you buy.

Anker’s Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W), model A110A, is the one power bank we’d buy if we could only own one. It’s expensive, at $229.99 at Anker as of October 26, 2026 (a sale price; Anker shows $30.01 off), and Macworld found it for $199.98 at Amazon in July. What you get for that is a battery with no real ceiling for everyday gear. Anker rates each of its two USB-C ports at 140W and the bank at 300W total, so it can fast-charge a 16-inch MacBook Pro and a second laptop at the same time and still run a phone off the 22.5W USB-A port.

Most banks make you wait as long to refill them as they took to drain. Anker rates the Prime at 50 percent in 13 minutes and 80 percent in 40 minutes, Anker’s page doesn’t say which setup those figures assume, but its fastest refill uses both USB-C ports at once with two 140W chargers, so expect slower results from a single charger. A built-in display shows the remaining charge and what each port is drawing, and the capacity is tuned for flying. At 26,250mAh, it comes in at 99.75Wh, just under the 100Wh line airlines use for carry-on batteries that don’t need approval. Expert Reviews, Engadget, and Macworld all ranked it at or near the top of their 2026 power bank roundups.

The trade is size. At 1.32 pounds, per Anker, it’s a bag battery, and if you only ever charge a phone, the UGREEN 20,000mAh bank below does that job for a quarter of the price. Check the model number before you buy, too. Anker also sold an older Prime 27,650mAh 250W bank (model A1340), which shows as sold out on Anker’s site, and the A110A is also sold in a bundle with a charging base. This recommendation covers the A110A power bank on its own.

A 20,000mAh battery is the size that covers the most situations without becoming a burden. It’s enough to recharge most phones more than once, top off a tablet, or buy a laptop a couple more hours, and it still slides into a backpack’s laptop sleeve. UGREEN’s Nexode Power Bank 20,000mAh 130W (model PB721) is the one we’d buy at that size. It costs $59.99 at UGREEN as of October 21, 2026, a sale price against a $89.99 list price, and UGREEN rates it for 130W of total output across two USB-C ports.

This is the successor to the 20,000mAh, 100W UGREEN bank that earned our travel award last time, and the predecessor’s results are why it’s back in that slot. In our testing, that model took an iPhone 16 Pro Max from empty to 55 percent in 30 minutes and to full in about an hour and a half, with 66 percent of the bank’s own charge left afterward. It also fully recharged a 2024 iPad Pro in two hours with 36 percent to spare. We haven’t run the same tests on the 130W version yet, so treat those as results from the previous model, not this one.

The feature we’d miss most on any other bank is the screen. It shows the remaining charge plus the voltage and current going to each device, so you can tell at a glance whether your laptop is actually fast charging or trickling along on a bad cable. The bank weighs about 480 grams, per UGREEN, and there’s no built-in cable, so pack a USB-C cable rated for 100W if you plan to charge a laptop with it. UGREEN’s US page names two USB-C ports; some international listings add a USB-A port, so check the listing if you still need one.

A magnetic battery snaps onto the back of an iPhone and charges it with no cable at all, which is why it’s the kind of power bank people actually carry every day. Anker’s MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro (model A110R) is the one to get right now. It costs $109.99 at Anker as of October 21, 2026, and it was $87.99 at Amazon during October’s Prime Big Deal Days. It’s built on Qi2.2, a newer version of the magnetic wireless standard that grew out of Apple’s MagSafe, and Anker rates it at up to 25W wirelessly and 45W through its USB-C port.

That 25W figure only applies to the iPhone 16 lineup and newer. Per Macworld, the iPhone 15 and older, plus the iPhone 17e, charge at 15W and the iPhone Air at 20W, and Anker excludes the iPhone 16e, which lacks MagSafe magnets. Macworld’s reviewer charged an iPhone 16 Pro to 50 percent in 30 minutes with the fan running. Faster wireless charging means more heat, and Anker’s answer is a small built-in fan with Cool and Silent modes. Reviewers at Macworld and Digital Camera World both found it audible up close, and Digital Camera World’s tester noticed the phone still got warm. If it bothers you on a nightstand, Silent mode turns the fan off.

The rest of the package earns the price. A fold-out kickstand props the phone up for video calls or watching something on a flight, the display shows battery level, temperature, and battery health, and 45W input means the bank itself refills quickly. Anker says it’s designed for Apple devices, so Android owners should look elsewhere, even though one reviewer did get a Pixel to charge on it. If you’d rather have a built-in cable than a kickstand, Ugreen’s MagFlow Pro is the rival Macworld compared it against. We have a MagGo 2 Pro on the way for a full review and will update this section with our own results.

Our previous multipurpose pick was the Anker PowerCore Fusion 10000. Anker’s current US lineup leads with a newer version, and the idea is unchanged. The Anker Power Bank (10K, Fusion, Built-In Cable), model A1637, is a 10,000mAh battery with folding wall prongs, so it works as a wall charger when you’re near an outlet and a power bank when you aren’t.

The new version adds a built-in USB-C cable, which fixes a familiar power bank problem: having the battery but not the cord. There’s also a second USB-C port for charging two devices at once, and Anker rates the output at up to 30W. That’s plenty for a phone, earbuds, or a tablet, but slow for a laptop. It costs $52.99 at Anker as of October 21, 2026, on sale, and B&H listed it for $44.99 the same day.

Like the model it replaces, it’s heavier than a normal wall charger, and in a loose hotel outlet, the weight can pull it partway out. If that happens, plug it into a power strip instead. For anyone who travels light, losing a separate charger from the bag is worth the trade.

If you work from coffee shops, libraries, or airport gates, the power bank that matters is the one that keeps your laptop alive until an outlet frees up. UGREEN’s Nexode 25,000mAh 145W Power Bank has been our pick for that since we tested it, and it’s still on sale at $79.99 at UGREEN as of October 21, 2026. UGREEN rates the battery at about 90Wh, which leaves it comfortably under the 100Wh limit for carry-on bags.

After using it regularly for months, it never let us down. It extended a 16-inch MacBook Pro by a few hours and fully recharged an iPhone 15 Pro Max and a Nintendo Switch OLED. It did run warm when a laptop drew power from it for long stretches, though never hot enough to worry us. A side display shows the remaining charge, so you know whether to plug it in before you leave.

One thing to know about the numbers: UGREEN’s product name says 145W, while its own product images list 140W, 65W, and 22.5W for the three ports. Either way, the main USB-C port has enough power to fast-charge most laptops, and the other two cover a phone and earbuds at the same time. The one thing it can’t do is run a laptop that only charges from its own AC adapter. For that, see the Goal Zero below.

Some gear still only charges from its own power brick: older laptops, camera battery chargers, a drone charger. The Goal Zero Sherpa 100AC gives you a real AC outlet, rated at 100W, in a bank that stays under the 100Wh carry-on limit. It costs $249.95 at Goal Zero and B&H as of October 21, 2026. Goal Zero shows that as a discount from $274.85.

The current model is the fourth-generation Sherpa 100AC, part number 22200. Beyond the outlet, it has two USB-C ports rated at 60W and 100W, two USB-A ports, and a 15W wireless pad on top. Goal Zero has sold several Sherpa generations under nearly the same name, and the previous one, model 22050, had a much weaker 5W wireless pad. Make sure the listing says 4th generation or 22200.

Know a couple of things before you buy. The AC outlet is modified sine wave rather than pure sine, which is fine for most chargers but can make some motors and audio gear hum or run poorly. Owner ratings are also mixed: REI showed a 3.9-star average across 63 reviews in October 2026, with some owners describing port and display failures. Goal Zero is now owned by BioLite, which bought the brand in April 2025 and has kept its products on sale. If you need more than about 100W of AC power, a portable power station is the better tool.

Our previous outdoor pick, Goal Zero’s Venture 75, was sold out at Goal Zero and Backcountry when we checked in October 2026, with no successor announced. For hiking and backpacking, we’d now carry the Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4. It’s a 10,000mAh battery that weighs about 5 ounces and carries an IPX7 rating, meaning it’s built to survive brief submersion, so rain, a creek crossing, or a soggy tent won’t kill it. It costs $83.95 at Garage Grown Gear as of October 21, 2026.

Weight is the whole point here. Most of the other 10,000mAh banks in CleverHiker’s 2026 testing weighed between 6.6 and 8.5 ounces, and on a multi-day trip, those extra ounces add up. Nitecore gets the weight down with a carbon fiber composite shell and silicon-carbon cells, and the bank has two USB-C ports with pass-through charging, so you can recharge it and your phone from one wall plug at a trailhead motel. It was the top backpacking pick in CleverHiker’s power bank testing this year.

It’s not a fast charger. Nitecore rates it at 22.5W, which is fine for a phone, a headlamp, or a GPS messenger but slow for a tablet. Like every power bank, it also delivers less than its label suggests, because energy is lost converting the cells’ voltage up to USB levels. If you’d rather recharge from the sun on longer trips, see our guide to the best solar power banks.

Sometimes you just want a cheap battery that won’t let you down. The Anker Zolo Power Bank (10K, 30W), model A1688, costs $29.99 at Anker as of October 21, 2026, and Amazon has sold it for about $22 in sales this summer. It has a 5.4-inch USB-C cable built in, a second USB-C port for another device, and enough capacity to get most people through a long day of heavy phone use.

We replaced our previous budget pick, a 10,000mAh INIU bank with a paw-print light, because it appears to match the INIU BI-B41 that the Consumer Product Safety Commission recalled in December 2025 after reports of overheating and fires. Only certain serial numbers were affected, but we’d rather not recommend a model with a recall on its record. If you already own one, check the serial number printed on the bank against INIU’s recall page.

Anker had recalls of its own in 2025, and the model number matters with this brand. The 10K Zolo we recommend here, the A1688, isn’t on either recall list. The Zolo 20K with built-in cables (models A1681 and A1689) was recalled in September 2025, so don’t assume the bigger Zolo is the same product. Check the model number printed on the back of any Anker bank you already own.

Every pick from our previous version of this guide either changed or left. Here’s what happened to each.

A power bank is a battery plus the electronics that turn its power into something your devices can use. These are the specs that separate a good one from a disappointing one.

Capacity is listed in milliamp-hours (mAh), measured at the cells’ own voltage, about 3.7 volts for most lithium-ion banks. Your phone charges at 5 volts or more, and converting between the two loses energy as heat. That’s why a 10,000mAh bank won’t charge a phone with a 5,000mAh battery twice. In Macworld’s 2026 capacity tests, 10,000mAh banks averaged 174 percent of a phone battery, not 200 percent.

Watt-hours (Wh) are the more useful number, because they don’t depend on voltage and they’re what airlines use. Multiply mAh by the cell voltage and divide by 1,000: a 20,000mAh bank at 3.7 volts is about 74Wh. As a rough guide, 10,000mAh covers a day of phone use, 20,000mAh covers a weekend or a tablet, and 25,000mAh or more is for laptops.

Output, in watts, decides how fast a bank charges your devices. Most current phones fast charge at 20W to 45W, tablets want 30W or so, and laptops need 45W to 140W depending on the model. Look for USB Power Delivery (USB PD) on the USB-C ports, since that’s the standard laptops and iPhones use, and check whether the advertised maximum comes from one port or is split across several. A bank rated for 100W total might only give 60W to each of two laptops.

Wireless power banks use the Qi standard. Qi2 added MagSafe-style magnets that line the phone up with the charging coil, and Qi2.2 raised the speed to 25W. Every iPhone since the iPhone 12 (except the 16e) has the magnets; Android support is spotty, and some phones need a magnetic case. Wireless charging is convenient but less efficient than a cable, so it gets more heat and fewer total charges out of the same battery. Our explainer on wired vs. wireless charging goes deeper, and our MagSafe accessories guide covers the cases, mounts, and wallets that use the same magnets.

Power banks have to go in your carry-on, never checked luggage. The FAA allows any number of batteries up to 100Wh, and up to two between 101Wh and 160Wh with airline approval. Airlines added rules of their own this year. Southwest allows one power bank per passenger as of April 2026, American and Delta cap passengers at two banks of 100Wh or less as of May 2026, and several airlines now bar power banks from overhead bins. International aviation rules adopted in March 2026 also limit passengers to two and ban recharging a power bank in flight. Rules are still changing, so check your airline’s page before you fly. Every pick in this guide is under 100Wh.

Power bank recalls have become common enough that checking is worth a minute. In 2025, Anker recalled more than 1.1 million PowerCore 10000 banks (model A1263) in June and about 481,000 more banks across five models in September. INIU recalled about 210,000 BI-B41 banks in December 2025. Recalls usually cover specific model and serial numbers, which are printed on the bank itself. Search the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s recall site for your brand.

Whatever you own, stop using a bank that’s swollen, cracked, or too hot to hold, and don’t charge one on a bed or couch where heat can’t escape. Buy from brands that sell under their own name and have a working support page, since they’re the ones that issue recalls and replacements when something goes wrong.

The Anker Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W). It costs $229.99 at Anker as of October 2026, can fast-charge two laptops at once, and stays just under the 100Wh carry-on limit. For less money, the UGREEN Nexode 20,000mAh 130W ($59.99) still charges a laptop, and iPhone owners who want a magnetic battery should get the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro.

As of October 2026, a good 10,000mAh bank from a known brand costs $25 to $60. Magnetic wireless banks cost $60 to $150. High-output laptop banks run $80 to $230, and banks with a built-in AC outlet cost $200 or more.

Yes, in your carry-on only. The FAA allows batteries up to 100Wh without approval, and some airlines, including Southwest, American, and Delta, now limit how many you can bring and where you can stow them. Check your airline’s rules before you fly.

Find the model number and serial number printed on the bank, then search the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s recall site and the maker’s support page. Recent recalls include Anker models A1263, A1257, A1647, A1652, A1681, and A1689 and the INIU BI-B41, though some recalls cover only certain serial numbers.

MagSafe is Apple’s magnetic charging system for iPhones. Qi2 is the open standard built on it, and Qi2.2 raised its top speed to 25W. A Qi2.2 power bank like the Anker MagGo 2 Pro charges an iPhone 16 or newer at up to 25W and most older iPhones at 15W.

No. Your phone controls how much power it accepts, and a power bank from a reputable brand only supplies what the phone asks for. If a bank delivers power badly or develops a fault, recent phones will slow down or stop charging and warn you.

Warm is normal, because some energy is lost as heat while charging, especially wirelessly. Hot is not. If a bank or your phone gets too hot to hold comfortably, unplug everything, move the bank away from anything flammable, and stop using it if it happens again.

Most power banks keep useful capacity for a few years of regular use, and many makers rate their cells for several hundred full cycles. Storing a bank about half charged in a cool place helps it age more slowly. Replace one that swells, no longer holds a charge, or gets unusually hot.

A dead phone at the wrong moment is more than an inconvenience. It can leave you unable to call for help, find your way home, or pull up a boarding pass. Pick a bank sized for what you actually carry, check its model number against recent recalls, and charge it before you need it. Then stop worrying about the battery icon.

#4726. GM to Pay $220 Million in Settlement After Alleged Privacy Violations

General Motors was reportedly selling millions of drivers’ data to insurance companies. Now, the company will fork over millions to 35 states and the District of Columbia.

General Motors is set to pay $220 million in a settlement with the attorneys general of 35 states and the District of Columbia after claims that the automaker sold drivers’ location and behavior data to brokers without permission.

GM’s Smart Driver program sits at the heart of the settlement. The driver monitoring system was meant to log driving data to help monitor driving habits, and was active between 2016 and 2024. However, the program regularly logged hard braking and speeding events, which GM then sold to data brokers under contracts that were used for insurance products, the group of attorneys general claims.

“The coalition’s investigation found that in reality, GM sold this information to data brokers under contracts that specified the data was to be used for insurance products. The data brokers sold the data to insurance companies, who could then change the drivers’ premiums based on their driving habits. GM did not disclose to drivers that their data would be sold for this purpose,” a statement from New York attorney general Letitia James reads.

“Safer, more helpful and personalized experiences are enabled by connected vehicle data, and GM is committed to being clear about what information is used, how it’s protected, and the choices customers have about what they share,” a GM spokesperson said to Reuters.

Over 370,000 drivers enrolled in Smart Driver weren’t even aware that the program was tracking their driving, the attorneys general claim. The OnStar app apparently said that they were not enrolled in Smart Driver before GM quietly un-enrolled them without notification. One driver even reportedly faced a 22 percent increase in insurance premiums because of “personal driving information provided by a data broker.”

Many customers signed up for Smart Driver at dealerships when purchasing a new vehicle; GM offered OnStar and Smart Driver as a one-step package deal to customers buying new vehicles, with heavy incentives for dealerships to increase sign-up rates. New York AG James claims that GM offered bonuses based in part on how many customers they signed up for GM’s connected vehicle services, including Smart Driver, and even ranked dealerships based on their enrollment numbers.

“People bought a car, not a tracking device,” as Oregon attorney general Dan Rayfield put it in a statement.

Settlement money will be doled out to consumers in Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Hawai’i, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Kentucky, Maine, Massachusetts, Maryland, Michigan, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia. GM previously paid $12.75 million to settle a California investigation into an alleged sale of drive data to brokers.

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4725. In 1828, serial killers sold their victims’ bodies to science

Published Oct 27, 2026 8:53 AM EDT

For as long as surgeons cut open living people to keep them alive, they have needed dead people to practice on. Today, donation programs keep medical schools supplied with the bodies they need to teach their students. But in 1820s Scotland, donating your body to science wasn’t legal yet. Nonetheless, one doctor found a way to get the bodies he needed. But it came at a terrible cost. This is the grisly story of the Anatomy Murders.

In the early 1800s, surgery was booming. A few decades earlier, Scottish surgeon John Hunter had helped bring a scientific view to Western medicine, transforming surgery with experimentation and careful observation. The Napoleonic Wars had boosted the demand for trained surgeons, Alun Evans, a retired epidemiologist at Queen’s University in Belfast, tells Popular Science.

One of the leading lights in this burgeoning field was Hunter’s compatriot Robert Knox, who ran an anatomy school in Edinburgh. But by 1827, Knox had hit a roadblock to his teaching ambitions. A change to regulations meant that dissection had become an important part of the medical curriculum. Knox’s school would require more than 400 bodies the following year. What made this such an overwhelming ask was that citizens had no legal way to donate their bodies to medical science. But where there’s a demand, supply will follow.

Edinburgh Medical School first opened in 1728, and for much of the next century, allegations of grave robbing linked to the school had been rife. Newly buried corpses would be exhumed and then presented at medical school doors by so-called “resurrectionists”.

The provenance of these bodies was unimportant to the corpse-strapped medical profession. But families, desperate to protect their loved ones, had taken extreme steps to stamp out the practice. Relatives would stay at their loved ones’ graveside for weeks, waiting for their bodies to lose their medical value. Factories produced devices like mort safes, heavy iron cages placed over newly dug graves. Knox had been forced to source his bodies from further away, even bringing some from across the Irish Sea.

Across the city, two other men also had a body problem. Irishman William Hare owned a lodging house with his wife near Edinburgh’s Grassmarket. One of his tenants was a fellow Irishman, William Burke. Burke and Hare became friends.

One day in early 1828, Hare discovered one of his tenants had died overnight. Even worse, the dead man still owed him rent. The pair came up with a plan to recoup the money, and they carried the corpse to Knox’s door. There, he paid them £7 and 10 shillings; more than a month’s wages.

Their eyes opened by greed, Burke and Hare hatched a plan to get Knox the bodies he desperately needed. Over the next 12 months, they brought him 16 fresh corpses. They had acquired each one by murdering their way through the poor of Edinburgh. They had lured the victims to Hare’s guesthouse, and then suffocated them in the night, lying on their chests to minimize any damage to their valuable bodies. The majority of their victims were women.

Burke and Hare’s rampage was only stopped in November 1828. A tenant at Hare’s guesthouse reported to the police that they had found a corpse under their bed. When the police raided the premises, they only found a single spot of blood where the body had been.

But under interrogation, Burke and his wife gave inconsistent accounts. Eventually, Burke, Hare, and their wives were all arrested.

Despite their equal guilt in their crimes, the two men had very different fates. Hare offered to confess everything to the authorities in exchange for his freedom. His evidence condemned Burke.

Two months later, Burke was hanged in front of a baying crowd. Ironically, his crimes meant that, under the Murder Act of 1752, he was not allowed a burial. His body was instead donated to the Edinburgh Medical School, where his skeleton is still on show today.

Hare disappeared after being freed. Evans says that research suggests he returned to Ireland, where some think he ended his days in Kilkeel Workhouse in County Down.

Knox faced graver consequences than Hare. He was never tried for his link to the murders, but his reputation was buried. He was forced out of a curatorial role at the Royal College of Surgeons and eventually moved to London. He was unable to secure another university teaching post, but continued to work as an anatomist at a hospital in the city.

Evans says the taint of the scandal went beyond Knox. “The Burke and Hare scandal really stymied medicine in Edinburgh considerably, and it explained the rising popularity of the Dublin schools and the Paris schools of medicine,” he says.

One fact that may have haunted Knox is that if he had avoided the lure of Burke and Hare’s corpses for just a few more years, he would have benefited from the Anatomy Act, passed in 1832, which gave surgeons the green light to procure any bodies from hospitals, prisons, or workhouses that had gone unclaimed for 48 hours. Voluntary donation was also legalized at the same time.

Instead, Knox became part of a black legend in Scotland’s history. Burke and Hare’s crimes have become an indelible part of Edinburgh’s grim past.

#4724. A three-legged cougar named Crimson is thriving in Arkansas

Published Oct 27, 2026 11:06 AM EDT

At first, the video seems to feature an empty habitat. There’s a crate filled with hay, platforms of various heights, and a ball hanging from a rope. Then a furry head peaks out from behind the crate. A few seconds later, a large wild cat bounds into view, rushing toward whoever is holding the camera. The young mountain lion (Puma concolor) appears so happy to see the videographer that you almost can’t tell he has only three legs.

“Crimson was just three weeks old when National Park Service biologists and then California Department of Fish and Wildlife determined he had been abandoned,” Emily McCormack, an animal curator at Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge in northwest Arkansas, tells Popular Science. “Using GPS collar data from his mother and camera monitoring, it was confirmed that she had moved to a different den site and was no longer returning to care for him.”

As if the situation could get any worse for the young mountain lion, he also had an injury to his hind foot. Without treatment, the injury ultimately could have killed him. He was rescued and transported to the Los Angeles Zoo, where he received acute veterinary care. Then he was taken to Oakland Zoo by Flying Tails animal air ambulance service. The Oakland Zoo veterinary hospital team eventually amputated the injured leg.

Thankfully, Crimson made an exceptional recovery, but he was too young to be considered for rehabilitation and release. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife decided Crimson would live permanently at Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge, a safe haven accredited by the Global Federation of Animal Sanctuaries. And now it seems safe to say that Crimson has settled well into his forever home.

“He is thriving in his new habitat at our sanctuary. We chose a long habitat enclosure with relatively flat ground, where he can explore but also has the ability to fully run a good distance,” says McCormack. “Crimson loves his neighbors, especially a female lion named Lucy. He loves his meal times and can be heard chirping all day to the staff, interns, and guests.”

Mountain lions, also known as cougars or pumas, are native to parts of the Americas and represent the world’s most wide-ranging cat species.

#4723. VW Suspends ID.Golf EV Development Amid Financial Pressures: Report

The electric Golf is apparently being put on the shelf, at least for now.

It was only a few months ago that Volkswagen was showing teasers of the next-gen electric Golf to folks behind closed doors, but a new report now claims development on said vehicle is suspended until further notice—a development pause that is one of the many cuts being made by the Volkswagen Group as it looks to save cash amid financial pressures.

The hatchback, which was exxpected to be named ID.Golf, was meant to be the electric successor to the ID.3. Reuters reports that it viewed a memo written by CEO Thomas Schaefer that revealed the delay. "I know what the Golf means for Volkswagen and for Wolfsburg. That's why this decision was really not an easy one for us," the internal memo reportedly said. “We simply can't afford this work right now.”

Whether or not Volkswagen would sell the supposed ID.Golf in the U.S. remains a question. We haven’t seen a standard Golf on sale here since the introduction of the current Mk.8 generation; the GTI and Golf R performance variants live on, thankfully, but an electric version sure would open the discussion back up to bringing the mainstream version to American shores again.

But the news is a large blow to those in Europe who might’ve been expecting a successor to the ID.3 before the end of the decade. VW recently revealed the ID.3 Neo (above) that brought sweeping changes to the car, at least ensuring there will be an electric, Golf-like car on sale across the Pond for some time. Still, the jump to the ID.Golf is meant to be a large one, as VW planned the new model along with a transition to a new Scalable Systems Platform (SSP) architecture.

The caveat to this news is that VW is expressing this as simply a delay in development. That means the company is still planning on picking things up at a later date, so presumably, an ID.Golf is still in the product roadmap. We just don’t know when it could arrive.

#4722. This lava planet shouldn’t have an atmosphere—but it does

Published Oct 27, 2026 11:32 AM EDT

The exoplanet TOI-561 b is fascinating to observe from 280 light-years away—but it’s not a place anyone would want to visit. Not only is it blanketed by an ocean of molten lava, but TOI-561 b is constantly bombarded by destructive radiation from its host star. The planet endures so much stellar energy that astronomers have long assumed its atmosphere evaporated eons ago.

However, new observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) contradict those initial conceptions. After examining TOI-561 b for 37 hours—almost four complete orbits—researchers now believe the planetary lava lamp actually features a thick atmospheric shell. The surprising evidence recently detailed in The Astronomical Journal isn’t what scientists assumed from a planet under such stellar duress.

“Our discovery challenges current theories,” said study co-author and University of Birmingham astronomer Anjali Piette. “We would expect a heavily irradiated rocky planet like TOI-561 b to have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago.”

Like Earth’s moon, TOI-561 b is tidally locked, which means its rotation coincides almost exactly with the time it takes to orbit its star. This ensures one side of the planet constantly experiences daylight, while its other half is always enveloped in darkness. JWST’s extensive observation window allowed Piette and her colleagues to study TOI-561 b’s phase curve—how its brightness and heat shift during its orbit. However, the results didn’t make sense. The planet’s dayside was cooler than it should be, while the nightside didn’t account for the temperature difference.

“[We] revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side,” explained University of Waterloo astrophysicist and study co-author Lisa Dang. “Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere.”

It’s likely not a thin layer of clouds, either.

“The evidence suggests it still has a significant atmosphere today,” added Piette.

Computer simulations of TOI-561 b’s climate indicate that its atmosphere is possibly composed of silicate minerals like silicon dioxide and magnesium silicate. If true, these would hypothetically reflect much of the harmful stellar radiation away from the planet’s surface. Regardless, the discovery creates more questions than it answers. It could be that TOI-561 b simply began with a huge quantity of gas. Another theory contends that the planet-wide molten ocean functions like a single, gigantic volcano that continually supplies gas into its atmosphere.

Armed with the new data, astronomers next hope to determine whether TOI-561 b resembles a hotter version of Venus that reflects about three-quarters of starlight, or if it operates like a superpowered iteration of Jupiter’s volcanic moon, Io. Either way, JWST will be called into service once again.“Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years,” said Dang.

#4721. Waymo adds nearly 250 square miles of robotaxi coverage in 5 cities

Waymo is growing its driverless service area by nearly 250 square miles over the next week, spread across Los Angeles, Nashville, Orlando, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

That’s about as big as Tesla’s entire Houston Robotaxi geofence after this week’s expansion, and Waymo is adding it in cities where it already runs with nobody in the driver’s seat.

The company announced the expansion in a short post on its blog today. Here’s what changes in each market, with Waymo’s updated service area maps:

Service now runs down the coast into the South Bay, through Manhattan Beach and Redondo Beach to Torrance.

The zone pushes further south, and riders can now get to the zoo.

Coverage on the east side nearly doubles, and there’s more service downtown.

The service area now stretches north to La Jolla, taking in University City and Clairemont along the way.

Waymo is pushing further into the South Bay, including a connection to BART at Berryessa station in San Jose. The service area now runs from San Francisco down the Peninsula to San Jose and Campbell.

Waymo didn’t break out square mileage by city, and it didn’t say how many vehicles it’s adding to cover the new ground. The updated maps are already in the Waymo app.

Some of these markets are very young. Waymo opened Nashville to public riders in April with a zone of about 60 square miles covering downtown, Midtown, Music Row, and East Nashville. San Diego only went public on September 1, with roughly 50 square miles between the beach and I-15 that barely crossed north of I-8. So getting to La Jolla less than two months later is a big jump.

In May, Waymo pushed its coverage past 1,400 square miles across 11 cities, which is bigger than the state of Rhode Island. Since then, it went driverless in Las Vegas, launched San Diego, and now says it operates in 15 US metros with more than 500,000 paid rides per week. It’s even mapping Toronto for a 2028 launch.

Tesla is also drawing bigger maps. After launching Robotaxi in Dallas and Houston with tiny geofences in April, it stretched Houston to about 254 square miles this week, according to Robotaxi Tracker. But the tracker counts 34 vehicles in Houston.

I'd like to see Waymo add more airports to their service list. Airports are huge drivers of both ride count and revenue for ride services. Waymo currently serves airports in some of their cities, such as Phoenix, San Francisco, and Nashville. However, other major airports such as LAX, Atlanta, and Dallas/Fort Worth do not currently have terminal service even though Waymo operates in those cities. Adding these might not look flashy on a map, but it would be a huge addition to Waymo's bottom line.

And on the metric that reflects actual use, it’s not close. Waymo logged 3.9 million rider-only miles per week in Q2 2026, while Tesla’s driverless fleet did 558,000 miles in its latest reported week, mostly in Austin. That’s about 7x, and it comes on the same day Elon Musk claimed the robotaxi race against Waymo “was never a real contest.”

I like this. Good progress. But I’ll be truly impressed when the Bay Area service area extends south into LA, expands north, and the same happens in San Diego.

It’s going to happen. Waymo is already dabbling with highway operations in California.I can see them linking all those service areas within the next 2 years. Maybe even by the end of next year if all goes well.
